slides.narration: Welcome to Book II, Chapter 14: Writing Functional-Style Code with Lambdas. This deck follows the Chapter 1 Slides model: concept on the left, code or evidence on the right, and presenter notes that tell the instructor what to say and do. Modern C++ is not about using the newest syntax because it looks impressive. It is about encoding ownership, lifetime, invariants, generic behavior, and failure boundaries so the program is easier to reason about and harder to misuse.

slides.narration: The learning target is professional explanation. Learners should be able to say what Writing Functional-Style Code with Lambdas changes about program design, not merely identify a keyword. Push for three layers: the intent, the mechanism, and the evidence. In modern C++, the evidence might be a destructor running, a copy becoming independent, a move leaving ownership in exactly one place, a constrained template rejecting a bad call, or an algorithm producing a predictable sequence.

slides.title: 14.1 Creating Lambda Expressions
keyPoints: A lambda expression creates a closure object with a callable operation.
Parameters describe call-time inputs; captures describe state obtained from the surrounding scope.
The distinction determines both behavior and lifetime.
Small lambdas are useful near algorithms because the operation stays close to the traversal that uses it.

slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 14, treat 14.1.2 Capturing Local Variables as a design decision with costs and evidence. [cutoff] copies the cutoff into the closure, producing a snapshot for this scalar. [&cutoff] borrows the original variable, so later changes are observed while that variable remains alive. The example changes cutoff from three to five and tests the difference with input four. A reference-capturing lambda returned from a function can dangle if it refers to an automatic local that has already ended. Capturing this also carries a lifetime dependency on the object; it is not an owning copy of all members. Prefer explicit captures where they clarify what escapes and who owns the needed state. slides.title: 14.2.2 Using Mutable Closures
keyPoints: A value-capturing lambda’s call operator is ordinarily const with respect to its captured members.
mutable permits modifying that closure state.
make_counter returns a lambda that owns its integer counter, so it does not borrow the factory’s local variable.
Copying the closure copies its captured integer, producing independent counter state.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 14, treat 14.2.2 Using Mutable Closures as a design decision with costs and evidence. A value-capturing lambda’s call operator is ordinarily const with respect to its captured members. mutable permits modifying that closure state. make_counter returns a lambda that owns its integer counter, so it does not borrow the factory’s local variable after return. Copying the closure copies its captured integer, producing independent counter state. A captured shared pointer would instead copy shared ownership and preserve a shared pointee. The closure’s copy behavior follows its member semantics just like any other object. The counter fixture uses only a few increments; an unbounded service counter would need an overflow policy. slides.title: Failure clinic — The callback outlived its capture
keyPoints: A function returns [&local] { return local; }.
The closure survives, but the referenced automatic object does not.
Calling the closure later uses an invalid borrow.
The repair is to capture an owned value, transfer an owner, or require a longer-lived external object.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 14, treat Failure clinic — The callback outlived its capture as a design decision with costs and evidence. A function returns [&local] { return local; }. The closure survives, but the referenced automatic object does not. Calling the closure later uses an invalid borrow. The repair is to capture an owned value, transfer an owner, or require a longer-lived external object. Adding const to the captured reference does not extend its lifetime. Another defect appears when a supposedly fixed configuration captures a shared pointer to mutable settings. The closure’s pointer value is fixed, but the settings can still change through another owner. A genuine snapshot may require copying the settings into an immutable value rather than copying only the owner. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.
